channel.title: Los Angeles Review of Books – Reviews
channel.description: Book reviews from the Los Angeles Review of Books.

item.title: Murky Effects
item.description: A novel of desire and domestic disorder amid a disintegrating literary establishment.

item.title: The Invisible Hand Job
item.description: Internet porn is the final frontier of surveillance capitalism.

item.title: A Swift Current Taking You Away
item.description: Whitney Strub’s new biography traces the complex trajet of leftist filmmaker Robert Kramer.

item.title: A Psychedelic Carnival of Nightmares
item.description: Paul Tremblay’s delirious new novel considers the ramifications of our technology- and media-saturated lives.

item.title: We Relax. We Take a Breath. We Can Begin to Think.
item.description: Solvej Balle’s series is about having the room and the time to really think.

item.title: California Sons: Miriam Pawel’s “The Browns of California”
item.description: Jake Wertz reviews “The Browns of California,” a four-generation biography of the Brown family and a portrait of the state they shaped.

item.title: Each Time Has Its Own Misfortune
item.description: Russian American author Nina Kossman offers a complex and thoughtful travelogue through a war-ravaged country.

item.title: Whimsical, Innovative Relationality
item.description: Yoko Tawada’s absurdist trilogy explores radical new modes of belonging beyond borders and biology.

item.title: God Bless Branson
item.description: James Steichen braves a trip to Branson, Missouri, to judge for himself the controversial entertainment mecca at the center of Joanna Dee Das’s new book.

item.title: The US Border Religion
item.description: Elizabeth Shakman Hurd examines how borders require acts of faith in something larger than the everyday.

item.title: Watching Artists Argue in Bars
item.description: Jessica Craig-Martin’s memoir is a coming-of-age send-up of 1970s and ’80s blue-chip bohemia.

item.title: Hanging on the Telephone
item.description: James Gleick’s history of the ‘telephone’ evokes an antique device most of us now barely recognize.

item.title: An Unlikely Contemplative
item.description: After a decade of sobriety, and years after leaving Christianity, Meghan O’Gieblyn finds herself relapsing into the pew and the bottle.

item.title: Pretend It’s Not Janet
item.description: In the first-ever biography of Janet Malcolm, the titular ‘absent woman’ is not the person you’d suspect.
